sections.label: Content note
sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses the sexual abuse of children by school staff, the death of a child in a wilderness program, and suicide. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.heading: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
Elite boarding schools are not part of the troubled teen industry, and Kids Over Profits does not track them as programs. Students apply to them for their academics. A school that takes children for their behavior or for therapy, or because a parent placed them there, is part of the troubled teen industry, whatever it calls itself. Day schools are not covered here.

But the two meet. The troubled teen industry took its name and its wilderness courses from boarding schools. The same consultants send children to both. And when elite schools finally investigated themselves, they found what we find in teen programs: children abused by the adults in charge of them, children who were not believed, and abusers sent on to the next school.

We are not the experts on boarding schools. Survivors, their lawyers and the organizations listed below have done this work. We keep [records of the schools](/related/elite-boarding-schools/), with the news about each.

sections.label: Where the wilderness program came from
sections.heading: Where the wilderness program came from
sections.body:
The wilderness programs we track descend from a boarding school. Kurt Hahn opened Gordonstoun, in Moray in the north of Scotland, in April 1934. In October 1941 he and Lawrence Holt, of the Blue Funnel shipping line, started the first Outward Bound course at Aberdovey in Wales.[^1] Wilderness therapy for teenagers was built on it. A 2000 study of four leading wilderness therapy programs found their methods "based on traditional wilderness programming ideas dating back to the 1960s in programs such as Outward Bound."[^2] Our [wilderness therapy timeline](/wilderness-therapy-timeline/) follows that line to the deaths in programs since.

Hahn's own school was not safe either. In June 2024 the Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry published its findings on Gordonstoun and its junior school, Aberlour. Lady Smith, who chairs the inquiry, found that children were abused there "in a variety of ways over a long period of time." A boy was raped by a staff member. "It was assumed the declaration of good intentions by founder Kurt Hahn was enough," she wrote. "At Gordonstoun, the assumption proved to be ill-founded, largely due to poor leadership."[^3]

sections.label: Borrowing the name
sections.heading: Borrowing the name
sections.body:
The programs we track also took the boarding school's name. Paris Hilton's parents sent her to them on a consultant's advice. "They were shown these beautiful brochures with kids smiling and on horses with rainbows in the background. They thought I was going to these amazing boarding schools, because that's what they were told," she told *Town & Country* in 2024.[^4]

[Agape Boarding School](/facility/agape-baptist-academy-mo/) in Stockton, Missouri, opened in 1996. It closed in January 2023, after dozens of former students went public with accounts of physical, mental and sexual abuse.[^5] The [John Dewey Academy](/facility/john-dewey-academy-ma/) in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, called itself a college preparatory school. It sat in a Victorian castle and charged $98,000 a year. *The Berkshire Eagle* described it as "geared for the coastal elite who are worried about their children's college prospects." Former students said its founder, Thomas Bratter, imposed strict diets and the wearing of "degrading cardboard signs for months at a time and even forcing them to dig their own graves." In 1998 Bratter was indicted after a 17-year-old student accused him of repeated sexual assaults. Under a plea bargain he received a suspended sentence and probation.[^6]

The resemblance ends at the door. The consultants' trade association says a stay at a therapeutic boarding school "can range from 12 months to 2 years depending on the program's therapeutic components."[^7] The program, not the school year, decides when a child goes home.

sections.label: The same consultants
sections.heading: The same consultants
sections.body:
The same consultants send children to both. The Independent Educational Consultants Association (IECA) prints one brochure for families choosing a boarding or day school, and another for "therapeutic placements."[^8][^9] When a child is "not succeeding in their current school, college, or home environment," the second asks parents: "When should we consider a residential school or treatment program?"[^9] At schools for students with emotional or behavioral needs, IECA says, "it is not uncommon for 25-75% of the student body to come from IECA member referrals."[^10]

The industry finds its customers among the families elite schools serve. "Educational consultants target high-net-worth families," Meg Appelgate, the chief executive of Unsilenced, told *Town & Country*, "and a lot of these consultants get kickbacks for referrals." "These parents are terrified that their kids are going to fall out of their social class," said Maia Szalavitz, the author of *Help at Any Cost*.[^4]

Clark Harman, 12, attended an elite private school in Manhattan before he was sent to [Trails Carolina](/facility/trails-carolina-nc/) in North Carolina.[^4] On his first night, February 2, 2024, counselors restrained him in a bivy sack zipped shut and fitted with an alarm, as the program's rules required for every new camper. He suffocated in it. The district attorney brought no charges.[^11] Our page on [referrers and educational consultants](/referrers-educational-consultants/) has more on how children are sent.

sections.label: Not believed
sections.heading: Not believed
sections.body:
A child who lives at school has only the adults there to turn to. "Boarding schools have an especially high duty of care because children live as well as learn there and may be separated from trusted adults outside the institution," Gabrielle Shaw, the chief executive of the National Association for People Abused in Childhood, told *The Guardian* in October 2026.[^12] When elite schools finally investigated themselves, they found how often that duty failed.

St. George's School in Middletown, Rhode Island, released its own investigation in December 2015. It found that three former employees had sexually abused 23 students, and admitted that it "failed on several occasions to fulfill legal reporting requirements." By January 2016 alumni said at least 40 victims had come forward. One of the three, Al Gibbs, was the athletic trainer from 1973 to 1980. Katie Wales, a former student, told reporters what a school official said when she reported him: "He looked at me and he said, 'You are just a distraught young lady, you are mentally unstable,' and didn't believe me and proceeded to completely ignore what I told him."[^13]

At the Thacher School in Ojai, California, a student told the school in the 1980s that her English teacher had repeatedly raped her from the age of 16. According to the school's own 2021 report, the assistant headmaster asked her whether she had "enjoyed" it. The school never called the police. The teacher resigned, and her college recommendation letter noted her "unfortunate involvement with a faculty member."[^14] At Emma Willard School in Troy, New York, Kat Sullivan "had been raped by a male teacher in 1998 only to be shipped off on a bus by school officials who sought to cover up the episode," the *Times Union* reported. The school's 2017 report traced sexual misconduct by its teachers back almost seven decades.[^15]

Jack Reid was 17 and a student at the Lawrenceville School in New Jersey when he died by suicide in April 2022. Students had spread a false rumor that he was a rapist. The school investigated and found no evidence, but never told Jack or his parents that he had been cleared. In 2023, in a settlement with his family, the school said that "actions taken or not taken by the school, likely contributed to Jack's death."[^16]

Teen programs write that disbelief into their rules. Agape Boarding School's handbook told parents: "If there is a question about a policy or rule, do not ask your son." A parent the school felt was "interfering with a student's progress" could be told to leave campus, and a parent who did not comply risked the son's expulsion.[^17] [Moonridge Academy](/facility/moonridge-academy-ut/), a Utah treatment program for girls, warned parents in 2008 that "it is common to hear horror stories from girls who are in residential treatment." A daughter's version, it said, "will likely contain only that amount of truth that defends her innocence and supports her manipulation."[^18] At St. George's one official refused to believe a girl. A teen program prints that refusal in the parent manual before the child arrives.

sections.label: Sent on with a reference
sections.heading: Sent on with a reference
sections.body:
When the schools did act, they often moved the problem on. Choate Rosemary Hall's 2017 report named 12 former faculty and staff members accused of sexual misconduct with students between 1963 and 2010. In some cases, it found, the school acted quickly; in others it did not.[^19] Loomis Chaffee in Windsor, Connecticut, learned in the 1990s that a former teacher, Paul Betts, had engaged in sexual misconduct with at least two students, and "did not report it at that time." Betts denies it. In a case from the 1980s, the school disclosed the allegations against another teacher only in "letters of recommendation" for him. In 1948 it wrote two references for Eric Meinecke, who was later named in an investigation at St. Andrew's School in Florida.[^20]

At Thacher, Michael Mulligan, a dean of students in the 1980s, hired a teacher who had had an inappropriate relationship with a student at another school, where Mulligan himself had reported him. The teacher was then accused of inappropriate conduct with several girls at Thacher.[^14] When St. George's fired Al Gibbs in 1980, it did not report him to any state agency.[^13]

Groton School in Massachusetts is the one whose silence ended in court. In 1999 a student's parents told the school that older students had sexually assaulted their son. The school said he had not given enough information to report. In April 2005 it pleaded guilty to failing to file an abuse report and was fined $1,250. No one was charged.[^21]

A child sent away to school, or to a program, has only the adults there to protect them. The schools' own reports show how often those adults protected the school instead.

If you know of an elite school, a consultant or a staff member with ties to a teen program, please [tell us](/contact/).

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If a child is in danger now**, call 911 (999 in the United Kingdom).
- **Abuse of a child at any school** in the United States can be reported to your state's child protective services agency or to the police. The [Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline](https://www.childhelphotline.org/), 1-800-422-4453, call or text, can help you find the agency to report to.
- **In the United Kingdom**, the NSPCC helpline takes reports about a child's safety, including at boarding schools: 0808 800 5000, or [report online](https://www.nspcc.org.uk/keeping-children-safe/reporting-abuse/).
- **Adults abused as children** in the United Kingdom can call [NAPAC](https://napac.org.uk/)'s support line, 0808 801 0331, Monday to Thursday 10am to 9pm and Friday 10am to 6pm.
- **Time limits on lawsuits.** [CHILD USA](https://childusa.org/) tracks each state's statute of limitations for child sexual abuse claims.
- **988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline**, 24 hours: call or text [988](tel:988).

For abuse in a youth program, see [our reporting directory](/report-abuse/).

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [SESAME](https://www.ncsesame.org/): Stop Educator Sexual Abuse Misconduct & Exploitation works to stop sexual abuse by school employees, supports survivors and campaigns against "passing the trash," the quiet moving of abusers from school to school.
- [CHILD USA](https://childusa.org/): A nonprofit think tank on child protection law; tracks every state's statute of limitations for child sexual abuse.
- [Boarding School Survivors](https://www.boardingschoolsurvivors.co.uk/): Founded in the United Kingdom in 1990; runs therapeutic workshops for adult former boarders, trains therapists and raises awareness of what boarding does to children.
- [Seen & Heard](https://seenheard.org.uk/): Founded in 2023 by former boarding school pupils; points people raised in boarding and independent schools to support.
- [NAPAC](https://napac.org.uk/): The National Association for People Abused in Childhood, the United Kingdom's support service for adult survivors of all forms of childhood abuse.

sections.label: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.heading: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.body: If you went to a boarding school or worked at one, and something here is wrong or missing, please [tell us](/contact/). We will correct it.
